newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FOCUS - Markets take Austria's vote in stride.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Markets take Austria's vote in stride.

text.p: Financial markets on Monday shrugged off a surge in far-right support in Austria's European parliament elections, and analysts called the strong Eurosceptic vote a one-off protest against tough budget cuts.

Austria's stock and bond market all but ignored Sunday's result. The Vienna bourse was steady in midday trading, with investors looking to Europe's leading markets for fresh clues. The bond market was holding to Friday's levels in limp trading.
"I don't really see any immediate effects on the market," said Alfred Reisenberger, Austria analyst at IMI Sigeco in London. "The vote ended in a draw."

Sunday's vote yielded a slim majority for the conservative People's Party, which inched ahead of its senior coalition partner, the Social Democrats of Chancellor Franz Vranitzky. The right-wing Freedom Party of Joerg Haider came third, but scored its highest-ever result in a nationwide election.

Haider had campaigned on a strong anti-Maastricht ticket, tapping rising discontent among voters over stinging welfare cuts and tax hikes designed to put Austria firmly on course for Europe's planned economic and monetary union (EMU).

But analysts said markets were reassured by the fact that about two-thirds of voters cast their ballot for parties which supported Austria's EU membership, almost mirroring the result of an EU referendum in June 1994.

"Once you take away the national focus, the cards are dealt completely differently. The main outcome really is a positive result for the pro-European parties," said a senior analyst at Creditanstalt-Bankverein in Vienna. "Two-thirds of Austrians are still for the EU -- that's not a very dramatic outcome."

While dealing the Social Democrats their worst nationwide score in Austria's democratic history, analysts said voters were unlikely to repeat such a massive protest in the next general election due in 1999.
"This is more about polemics than anything else. The 1999 elections are so far away that this will hardly have any effect," said Reisenberger.

"Sure the Haider effect was the most significant. But the markets take this pretty much in their stride," added Michael Claus, Austria analyst at CSFB in London. "It would have been much more worrying if Haider had overtaken the conservatives."

The People's Party won 29.6 percent of the vote, followed by the Social Democrats at 29.1 percent. The far-right notched up 27.6 percent, a huge jump from the five percent it commanded when Haider took over the party 10 years ago.
Austrians were widely expected to blame Brussels for their economic headaches, including a record wave of insolvencies and rising unemployment.

But financial analysts maintain most of the issues are home-grown, and said EU membership had just helped to expose Austria's underlying problems of growing uncompetitiveness, a bloated bureaucracy and excessive government spending.
